title: The Change of Control Clause That Can Stall Your Sale After You've Already Agreed a Price
excerpt: A price gets agreed and the term sheet is signed. Then a clause in the lease or a key customer contract needs someone else's consent, and the deal stalls at the worst possible moment.
content:
The price gets agreed. Everyone is pleased with the number. The owner and the buyer shake hands, or at least exchange the modern equivalent, a signed letter of intent and a bottle of something good put aside for settlement day. Then the buyer's lawyers start reading the fine print of every material contract the business runs on, and a clause nobody thought twice about for the last ten years suddenly becomes the thing the whole deal turns on.

It is rarely the financials that cause this kind of stall. Most owner-led businesses selling for the first time have their numbers in reasonable shape by the time a term sheet lands. What catches owners out is a change of control clause sitting quietly in the commercial lease, the biggest customer agreement, the equipment finance contract or the bank facility, a clause that says ownership cannot change hands without someone else's consent first.

This is not a flaw in how the business was run. These clauses are standard, and from the other party's point of view, entirely reasonable. The problem is timing. The moment a business owner finds out about one is usually the worst possible moment to find out about it.

Where these clauses actually live

A change of control clause does what the name suggests. It gives a landlord, a lender, a key customer or a franchisor the right to be asked, and sometimes the right to say no, before the business they have a contract with changes hands. For an owner-led SME, this shows up more often than most people expect: in the lease on the premises, in the facility agreement with the bank, in the supply contract with the business's largest customer, and in franchise or distribution agreements that were signed years before a sale was ever on the radar.

Whether the clause actually gets triggered depends on deal structure. A share sale, where the legal entity itself is sold and simply changes owners, trips far more of these clauses than an asset sale, where the buyer purchases the operating assets and the contracts are typically re-papered or novated from scratch. That structural difference is one reason the exit readiness conversation needs to start well before a term sheet, not after one.

Why it surfaces at the worst possible time

The pattern we typically see is consistent. Due diligence is where these clauses get found, and due diligence happens after the price has already been agreed and the emotional investment in the deal closing is at its highest. That is exactly the moment the party whose consent is needed has the most leverage and the least reason to move quickly. A landlord asked to consent to a change of control might use the moment to push for a longer lease term or a rent increase. A key customer might use it to renegotiate pricing. None of this is done in bad faith. It is simply a predictable use of leverage by someone who suddenly has some.

The result is rarely a dead deal. It is usually a delayed one, a renegotiated one, or one where the seller ends up giving something back at the exact point they have the least appetite to push back. It also unsettles a buyer's confidence in everything else they have been told about the value drivers behind the business, at precisely the point where confidence is what keeps a deal moving to settlement.

The fix is timing, not avoidance

These clauses cannot be negotiated out of existence after the fact, and trying to remove them from every material contract years in advance is not a realistic use of anyone's time. What actually works is knowing they exist before a buyer's lawyers find them. That means pulling together an index of the handful of contracts that matter most, the lease, the facility agreement, the top two or three customer contracts, and reading the assignment and change of control clauses in each one, ideally twelve months or more before the business goes to market.

This is one of the eight dimensions a proper exit readiness diagnostic is built to score, alongside things like customer concentration and owner dependence, because a contract surprise mid-negotiation does more damage than the one clause in question.

Where a consent is genuinely going to be needed, there is often a quiet way to open that conversation with the landlord or the key customer well ahead of a live deal, framed as a routine business matter rather than a signal that a sale is imminent. Owners who do this arrive at due diligence with the hard part already handled.

None of this is something a bookkeeper or compliance accountant would flag, and that is not a gap in what they do. Their work is the ledger, the lodgements and the numbers being accurate, not the structural read of what sits inside a stack of commercial contracts. That is a different lens entirely, and it is usually easier to apply with someone looking at the business from the outside, well before a buyer's name is on the table.

faqs.q: What is a change of control clause in a business sale contract?
faqs.a: A change of control clause is a provision in a lease, loan or customer contract that requires consent from the other party before ownership of the business can change hands. These clauses are common and usually reasonable, but they need to be identified before a sale, not during due diligence when they carry far more leverage. An exit readiness diagnostic is designed to surface them early.

faqs.q: Can a landlord stop the sale of a business on leased premises?
faqs.a: A landlord generally cannot stop a sale outright, but many commercial leases require their consent before the tenant entity changes hands, and that consent can come with conditions attached, such as a longer lease term or a rent review. It is rarely used to block a sale, more often to extract a better position for the landlord at the point of highest leverage.

faqs.q: Do change of control clauses apply to asset sales as well as share sales?
faqs.a: Less often, and that is one reason deal structure matters early in the conversation. A share sale transfers the existing legal entity and its contracts as they stand, which is exactly what triggers most change of control clauses. An asset sale usually involves re-papering or novating contracts with the buyer, which sidesteps many of these clauses but introduces its own timing and consent requirements.

faqs.q: How early should an Australian SME owner review contracts before selling?
faqs.a: Twelve months out is a reasonable rule of thumb, well ahead of any live negotiation with a buyer. That gives enough time to read the assignment and change of control clauses in the lease, the bank facility and the largest customer contracts, and to open any necessary conversations quietly. Reviewing contracts for the first time during due diligence is the scenario that causes the most avoidable delay.

faqs.q: What happens if a major customer contract has a change of control clause?
faqs.a: The customer typically needs to be asked to consent before the sale can complete, which is a delicate conversation if the customer does not yet know the business is being sold. Handled early and framed as routine, it rarely causes a problem. Discovered for the first time mid-negotiation, it can slow settlement or give the customer room to renegotiate terms at the worst possible moment.

faqs.q: Can a hidden contract clause actually reduce the price a buyer pays?
faqs.a: Indirectly, yes. A clause that surfaces late in due diligence rarely changes the valuation methodology itself, but it can unsettle a buyer's confidence and give them a reason to ask for a price adjustment, an extended settlement period, or holdbacks tied to resolving the consent. A business valuation done with the contract position already mapped avoids that kind of late surprise entirely.

faqs.q: Who should review a business's contracts before it goes to market?
faqs.a: Ideally someone outside the day to day running of the business, since owners are often too close to contracts they have not reread in years to spot where the risk sits. This sort of structural review sits alongside financials, customer concentration and owner dependence as one of the standard checks before a sale, and it pairs naturally with broader exit readiness preparation.
